profile.reading:
This building at 7301 Metropolis Drive, in the Met Center business park in southeast Austin, Travis County, is CyrusOne's second data center in the Austin market, generally referred to by the company and in trade press as Austin II or AUS2. Met Center sits roughly seven minutes from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport and has become one of CyrusOne's longer running Texas campuses alongside its Dallas area and Houston sites. Trade press coverage from August 2014 describes CyrusOne adding 5,000 square feet of white space to Austin II's second data hall, bringing the building to roughly 65,000 square feet at that time, and describes the building as the first phase of what CyrusOne then planned as a potential four phase campus totaling 290,000 square feet, backed by 22 acres the company acquired in Austin that year. Whether that specific four phase plan was carried out as originally described is not confirmed by any source found here. What is documented is that CyrusOne later built a third Austin facility, Austin III, on a separate address nearby at 7100 Metropolis Drive, announced in April 2015 as up to 172,000 square feet of shell space with up to 120,000 square feet of colocation space and up to 12 megawatts of power, described at the time as the company's largest facility in the Austin market.

CyrusOne's own current marketing page for its Austin campus describes AUS2 and AUS3 together, stating 242,000 square feet of combined IT technical space and 19 megawatts of combined total IT power capacity across both buildings, alongside SSAE 16, PCI DSS, HIPAA, ISO 27001, and FISMA compliance, TIA-942 design standards, and a claim of zero water consumption for cooling. That 19 megawatt figure is explicitly a two building campus total, not a per building disclosure, so it is recorded here as campus context rather than assigned to this building alone. No source found in this research session breaks the combined 242,000 square feet or 19 megawatts down between AUS2 and AUS3 individually, and no operator disclosure more recent than the 2014 figure above addresses this single building's own current square footage. Utility power, IT critical load, standby generation, and any onsite generation capacity specific to this building are not separately disclosed by CyrusOne in any source found here.

No zoning case, tax abatement filing, or contested hearing specific to this address was found in Austin or Travis County records, consistent with Met Center's status as an established, already zoned business and industrial park rather than a site requiring new rezoning for a data center use. The building sits within a city now actively debating new rules for the data center industry broadly. Austin City Council opened work in August 2026 on a dedicated data center zoning classification and a formal position against incentivizing new data center construction, per Texas Tribune reporting, driven chiefly by concern over prospective large hyperscale campuses elsewhere in the region rather than by this smaller, established facility, which was not named in any account of that debate found.

reading.body:
CyrusOne Austin II occupies one building of a two-building campus at 7301 Metropolis Drive in Travis County. The AUS2-AUS3 campus publishes 19 MW of total IT capacity across 242,000 square feet, but no per-building breakdown exists, so this facility's individual load is not confirmed. At a typical AI training density of 40 kW per rack, 19 MW would sustain roughly 475 racks, though this figure covers both buildings and should not be attributed to Austin II alone.

The campus holds SSAE 16, PCI DSS, HIPAA, ISO 27001, and self-reported FISMA certifications. These qualifications allow the site to serve security-sensitive and regulated workloads, though no specific tenants or workload types are published.

Texas publishes capacity figures for only 18 of its 133 mapped data center facilities, totaling 468 MW. The AUS2-AUS3 campus ranks 19th in published capacity statewide, below the published tier but consistent with CyrusOne's strategy of expanding colocation in Texas markets where state tax policy and fiber infrastructure position the operator as a major regional player.
